content: Multi-floor indoor routing literature supports a single connected graph with explicit vertical transitions rather than stacked per-floor graphs. Ariadne (Aug 2026) states vertical transitions are 'not interchangeable edges': they differ by capability (stairs exclude wheelchairs/prams, escalators exclude trolleys), by cost (lift wait time is a real variable cost), by direction (one-way escalators/doors) and by disorientation (every transition resets the visitor's mental map, so the first instruction after arrival matters most). 'A router that treats floors as stacked copies produces routes that are technically connected and practically hostile.' Accessibility is 'a routing mode, not a filter' - the step-free route is a genuinely different route, not the default minus stairs. Academic precedents: MIT Whiting et al. (2006) model stairs and elevators as source/destination nodes in one topological data model; Lorenz et al. (2006) propose hierarchically structured graphs with typed edges; Stoffel et al. (2008) apply hierarchical graphs to pedestrian indoor navigation.
